extracted.intended_audience: public broadcasters, public media leaders, funders/grantmakers, podcasters and audio journalism strategists
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria about how podcasting and on-demand audio can serve the public interest, aimed at public media organizations, funders, and producers deciding strategy, programming and infrastructure investments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Podcasting's public-interest potential
rubrics_metrics.description: Podcasting and other forms of on-demand audio have the potential to foster a media landscape that lifts up the hidden stories and absent narratives of our diverse society, that reflects local communities, and that provides an open and accessible platform for innovation that can serve democracy’s future generations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is framed as potential rather than guaranteed outcome — realizing it "will take work, vision and compromise." Use podcasting to surface underrepresented narratives and local perspectives, but recognize effort and intentional strategy are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reach younger listeners and creators
rubrics_metrics.description: One notable finding is the age difference between podcast listeners and the legacy public radio audience. Knight organizations corroborated third-party research showing that young adults (approximately 25 to 34 years old) represent a majority of on-demand listeners. This age cohort not only listens to podcasts, but also avidly creates them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate podcast initiatives by their ability to reach and engage younger demographics both as audience and creators; consider targeted recruitment, format and platform choices that appeal to 25–34-year-olds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enable new, diverse creators to find voices
rubrics_metrics.description: Podcasting is allowing a younger and sometimes more diverse generation of public-interest creators to find their voices, testing innovative approaches to both journalism and storytelling in the process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support pipelines for diverse talent (inside and outside public broadcasting). Examples: WNYC, Gimlet Media, independents like W. Kamau Bell. Consider partnerships and flexible relationships (e.g., creators who dip in and out of public broadcasting).

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop programming freed from the broadcast 'clock'
rubrics_metrics.description: The open field allows legacy producers to identify and collaborate with new people and partners, develop story formats that are freed from the rigid broadcast 'clock' that defines the pubcasting dial, and diverge from the predictable tone and pace of public radio.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess shows on whether they exploit on-demand format advantages (variable length, pacing, narrative forms) rather than mimicking broadcast constraints; encourage experimentation in story form and tempo.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use new distribution tools to break on-air conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Knight-supported apps such as NPR One and WNYC’s Discover are providing new ways to distribute content that breaks on-air conventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider distribution strategies (apps, platforms) as part of program quality — apps that surface tailored content or break broadcast norms can extend reach and engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design audio to be on-demand, portable, and context-sized
rubrics_metrics.description: These shifts point to a future where narrative audio is reliably on demand, portable across platforms, and sized to fit different contexts and moods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether content is produced/packaged to be consumed in different contexts (commute, short breaks, deep listening) and whether it is portable across platforms and devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance consumer choice with shared national news experience
rubrics_metrics.description: This bodes well for consumer choice, but less well for the project of building a shared national news experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize trade-offs: prioritize both audience choice and mechanisms to sustain shared civic conversation; measure impact on public information commons, not just downloads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate personal, distinctive narrative storytelling
rubrics_metrics.description: Forward-looking Knight partners within the public radio system are seeking out creative makers with a personal and distinctive approach to narrative storytelling, one that can connect with an audience eager for new sounds and new work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize commissioning and promoting hosts/producers with unique voices and perspectives (examples: Radiotopia, 'Millennial', 'Strangers', WNYC's 'There Goes the Neighborhood'). Assess programs by distinctiveness and audience connection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Represent geographic and ideological diversity, not just urban voices
rubrics_metrics.description: Such an environment highlights the challenges of how to represent the full spectrum of voices and perspectives across a highly polarized nation. Diversity cuts both ways. Simply including more diverse perspectives from urban centers does not serve those members of the public living in rural and exurban areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure diversity along multiple axes (geography, ideology, class) and emphasize strategies that reach beyond urban centers; invest in deeper listening across divides to avoid narrow representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice deeper listening across political and social divides
rubrics_metrics.description: If this election has revealed anything, it’s the need for deeper listening across divides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Programs should be evaluated by their capacity to foster listening and understanding across polarized communities — consider editorial practices, outreach and story selection that prioritize cross-divide engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage nimble digital-first production and experiment with revenue models
rubrics_metrics.description: For digital-first producers that are launching outside the confines of public broadcasting, it’s full speed ahead. These creative organizations can move quickly and nimbly to seek out and serve the on-demand audience. Without expensive broadcast infrastructure or the need to satisfy the expectations of an established audience, digital startups represent a dynamic opportunity to innovate within different organizational structures. Benefit corporations, for-profits, and non-profits are all vying for the ears of audiences and testing new revenue models to sustain public interest programming.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess organizations on agility, experimentation, and viability of revenue strategies; consider organizational form (for-profit, benefit corp, non-profit) in sustainability planning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increase agility, diversity and collaboration across public broadcasting system
rubrics_metrics.description: Public broadcasters risk losing their leading position, due to lack of agility, diversity and collaboration across a balkanized national-to-local system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate institutional reforms and partnerships that increase speed, diversify staffing and content, and improve collaboration between national and local entities to avoid fragmentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build a functional public-interest infrastructure for digital audio
rubrics_metrics.description: In the report’s appendix, we lay out the elements needed to comprise a more functional public interest infrastructure for digital audio, and show what progress has been made on each of these elements. If the public broadcasting system does not step up to knit these pieces together, commercial distributors will continue to dominate the podcast landscape, and the chance to build a platform based on mission rather than monetization will be lost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess progress against concrete infrastructure elements (as outlined in the report appendix): coordination, distribution, funding, talent pipelines, measurement and standards that support mission-driven audio. Prioritize knitting together pieces to maintain mission over pure monetization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funders and large public media should seek out and amplify diverse talent
rubrics_metrics.description: This report shows that much more can be done by grantmakers and by the country’s largest public media producers to seek out, encourage and amplify the diversity of talent with potential to serve the public interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Funders should be evaluated by their proactive outreach, support (grants, training, promotion) and amplification strategies for diverse audio creators; public media should measure success by talent discovery and audience impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Podcasting is not a silver bullet
rubrics_metrics.description: Podcasting attracts new voices and audiences to public media, but it’s not a silver bullet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use realistic evaluation criteria — podcasting can advance public-interest goals but cannot alone solve structural problems; pair podcast initiatives with broader strategic investments and policy changes.
